B is clean and honest, with sourced benchmarks and careful caveats. But its plays are generic: a kit and templates. Its 'proven mechanic' claims rest on Typeform and Tally. Its forecast applies ChartMogul free-to-paid rates to modeling units, and the 100-company pool is invented.
B's plays are less actionable, and its January workshop audience is an unsupported hypothesis. Its $400 ad cap is weakly justified given its own admission that the economics are poor.
truthX: Several numbers are assumptions (about 400 wall-clicks, 80% margin, $50/hour, 4% reply rate), though they are labelled as such.
Some claims, such as the 'service plan sells better' analogy, rest on weak support, though they are flagged as assumptions.
Details about Tally's reviews and competitors' MCP support are cited, and I cannot verify them.
truthY: The 100 eligible companies figure is invented, though it is called a modeling unit.
Applying the ChartMogul six-month freemium conversion benchmarks to 90-day cohorts is shaky, though it is disclosed.
The workshop and January audience is an unsupported hypothesis, though it is labelled as one.
The claim that the mechanics are proven rests on competitor examples rather than on Formkit results, though this is disclosed.

reasons: A is unmistakably built for Formkit. It identifies that monetisation, not traffic, is the constraint, and backs that with a stated falsifier. It anchors every channel on a differentiator ('no cut on Stripe payments', 'looks like yours') rather than 'free', where Tally and Google Forms already compete.

A gives the owner ready-to-use assets: in-product upgrade screen copy, the follow-up email, an agency cold email with a done-for-you sample offer, and Claude directory listing copy. B provides no publishable copy at all.

A's unit economics are explicit: about $58 gross profit per Pro seat in year one, break-even reply and conversion rates, and a rule that yearly Pro or Business must lead any paid traffic. Those numbers justify keeping ads at $0, and the conditional search test has sensible guardrails, including the FormKit Vue name-collision negatives.

A's plays are non-obvious but rest on proven mechanics: a trigger-based agency outreach list mined from rival reviews, and an early listing in a new connector directory. Each has numeric kill and scale rules and owner-hour budgeting.

B is honest and well cited (ChartMogul, WordStream), with good caveats. Its plays are generic, though: upgrade prompts, template SEO pages and an AI guide, all reported per 100 workspaces. It lacks specificity, positioning and execution detail.
B's SEO template play is slow to pay back within 90 days for a non-expert owner, and B does not address the low per-seat economics beyond a caveat.
truthX: Several 'confirmed' claims, such as yearly billing giving two months free and chat build-and-publish working on the free plan, rely on site insights that are not shown and cannot be verified here.
It claims Tally's help page points users who want branding and payments to other tools. This is a characterisation of a source that may be overstated.
The ad-test kill criteria are inconsistent: the portfolio note uses $58 per Pro account, while the experiment uses $6 per signup.
Some funnel numbers (about 400 wall-clicks, 60 installs) are labelled assumptions, but the P50 forecasts are built on them before any baseline exists.
truthY: The ChartMogul report is cited as '2026', and its 8% median free-to-paid figure is applied to a very different price point. The mismatch is acknowledged, but the figure still drives the day-90 target of 8.
The day-90 target of 8 is not derived from any Formkit data, which B itself admits.

reasons: A is far more specific to Formkit: it centers on the free-to-Pro paywall moment (payments with no cut, own domain, badge removal), which fits the unlimited free tier and the $6 Pro price.

A does real unit economics: affordable CAC, $58 first-year gross profit per Pro seat, break-even per play, and the conclusion that monthly Pro can't fund paid traffic. B only says low per-seat pricing makes ads risky.
A's kill/scale thresholds, minimum sample sizes, guardrails and stopping rules are concrete and tied to break-even. B's rules are vaguer.

A names the FormKit Vue library name collision and adds negative keywords. It also notes that Tally, Jotform and Typeform already support MCP, so it positions on no-cut payments rather than 'free in chat'. Both show strategic awareness B lacks.
A includes ready-to-use copy: upgrade screen text, follow-up email, cold agency email and directory listing copy. B has none, despite the 'publishable copy' rule.
A labels nearly every estimate as an assumption with a grade and has a falsifier for its diagnosis, plus an honest P10/P50/P90 with low confidence on riskier plays.

B is honest and cites ChartMogul and WordStream, but its play scenarios are generic (templates SEO, AI guide) with big assumed traffic numbers and no basis for the traffic. SEO-style plays are slow for 90 days, and its 8-account target is arbitrary.

B's 8% free-to-paid median comes from companies with much higher ARPA, and it admits this is only directional. It is an unreliable basis for a $6 product. B also leaves $450 of budget 'reserve' with little plan to use it.
truthX: Unsupported assumptions like about 400 wall-clicks, 6% conversion, 4% reply rate and 80% margin are labeled as assumptions, but they still drive the forecasts.
The 'two months free' yearly pricing and the Stripe no-cut claim are stated as confirmed facts that can't be checked here.
Some cited URLs, such as the Tally help page and the claude.com docs, can't be verified from the text.
truthY: The 8% median free-to-paid benchmark and the 5-in-1,000 example are applied to a $6/seat product, even though the source's customers have much higher revenue per customer. B flags this, but the modeled results still rest on it.
The visit volume scenarios (300/800/1,600 and 100/300/700) are invented assumptions with no basis in Formkit data, though labeled as assumptions.
The portfolio total of 4/14/42 sums arbitrary assumptions and implies precision it doesn't have.

climbos.topIssue: The plan contradicts itself in ways the owner can't resolve alone. The positioning, audience notes and experiment all say to lead with no-cut payments, not 'free', yet the shipped directory listing and agency email both lead with free. The search test also carries two different kill rules: $6 per signup in the experiment versus $58 per Pro with a 3-Pro scale bar in the portfolio note, which the plan itself says the budget can't reach.

luna.topIssue: The plan is carefully hedged and sourced but delivers no ready-to-use assets (no upgrade prompt copy, no template page draft, no AI-assistant guide outline), so the owner gets a measurement framework rather than executable growth plays.

sol.topIssue: Despite the rule that publishable copy be ready to use, the plan supplies no ad copy, partner outreach messages, in-product upgrade prompts or landing-page text, so a non-expert owner must still write every customer-facing asset; the eight-company target also exceeds the five-company likely acquisition case if no existing eligible pool exists.

reasons: A cites a specific page for every claim, such as a contact, CRO or Chicago Cause page, so the owner can quickly check each first line. B cites only homepages for very specific dated details (sessions on Oct 19–21, a $5–$20 price, a deadline). That makes B's evidence much harder to verify and raises the risk of errors.

A is candid that most prospects lack a dated buying trigger and scores timing low. B's trigger logic looks strong but is shaky. An event that runs tomorrow (Forecast Pro, Oct 19–21) or within two weeks already has its registration built. B's 90–95 timing scores overstate how urgently these prospects need a new form tool.

B is more actionable on the surface. It gives named contacts and public emails, and its event/training ICP fits a form builder's payment and registration features well. That is a real strength over A, which supplies roles only and no addresses.

A's sequence is coherent and pitches a concrete deliverable (an intake outline based on the prospect's services). B's Day 0 email packs in features, plan limits and pricing, so it reads like a spec sheet. B's first lines mostly just restate an event date and lack an insight-driven hook.
A's agency ICP plausibly fits Pro (custom domains, connections) and flags free-plan cannibalization risk. Both handle compliance responsibly, and B also documents an exclusion.
truthX: Fit scores of 68–88 are presented with false precision, though they are labeled as judgments.
A few first lines are flat observations rather than hooks; this is a craft weakness, not a truth problem.
truthY: Highly specific event dates, prices, deadlines and stats (33,000 AEC customers, 200+ events per year) are cited only to homepages, so the claims cannot be verified from the cited sources.

Pricing and plan claims in the email copy ($6 per seat, unlimited free forms, responses and members, Stripe payments, version history) are risky to send. Their accuracy cannot be confirmed from what is shown here.
Timing scores of 85–95 overstate urgency for events whose registration is already live or that happen within days.

reasons: B's prospects carry dated, near-term triggers (specific November workshops, deadlines, a December webinar), so the 'why now' is real and the timing scores are credible. A admits most of its prospects have no dated trigger and gives them timing scores of 25-40.
B's first lines cite concrete public details (dates, pricing, form fields) and read as personal. A's lines are generic observations about contact pages and could apply to any agency.

B gives named contacts and public emails for most prospects, so the owner can send immediately. A deliberately gives no emails and mostly gives only role guesses, which leaves the owner more research to do.

B's email copy is more specific to Formkit: it mentions pricing, a free plan, payments through the owner's Stripe account, the logic map and drop-off metrics, and it has a clear low-risk ask. A's emails are vaguer and tell the prospect to 'consider an outline', which is weaker.
B flags a date discrepancy for DMI, excludes MBX Events for its no-spam terms, and raises UK PECR, which shows careful diligence. A's compliance notes are good but its fit logic is weaker.
A's agency ICP is coherent, but several of its prospects (Webstacks, Solid Digital, Clay) are admitted to be poor fits because they likely have their own stack, which weakens the list.
truthX: Claims that Formkit's feature set (custom domains, connections) is confirmed rest on the homepage only; this is minor.
Cites Amply as 34 people and Orbit as 50+; these are plausibly sourced, so there are no clear fabrications, but several contact-title guesses are speculative.
truthY: Pricing ($6 per seat) and free-plan details are stated in the email copy; they are cited to the pricing page but should be verified before sending.
Event dates, workshop details and emails are all cited to homepage URLs rather than specific pages, so they are hard to verify.
DMI's date discrepancy is acknowledged but unresolved.
Some job titles and public emails (such as Icenhower's info@icenhowercoaching.com domain mismatch) may be unverified.

reasons: B delivers what was asked: 10 named prospects, each with cited URLs, a 4-step sequence and a first line for every company. A delivers 4 holds, none sendable, and only 3 first lines. The owner can act on B this week; A mostly hands them a research to-do list.

A's ICP is strategically sharper for a $6/seat tool. Solo-to-15-person studios whose branded inquiry form is the client's first step are a tight fit, and its openers are concrete (Rocky West's four separate forms plus Typeform, Thirteen's spam warning).

B's targeting is weaker. Several picks (Orbit 50+, Clay, Ramotion, Webstacks) are sophisticated web agencies that build forms in their own stacks, and B admits this in places. Fit scores in the 80s look inflated against that.
B's first lines are mostly flat restatements of a contact page with no tension. Its sequence is coherent and offers a useful free brief structure, but it is generic.

A's process discipline is excellent: it refuses to pad the list, sets verifiable qualification gates and gives compliance notes. That honesty does not make up for zero usable output in a 90-day revenue push.
Neither supplies verified email addresses. B names one decision maker (Jeremy Durant); A names none.
truthX: Sequence claims Formkit features (AI form building, AI-written personal replies, Claude/ChatGPT integration, partial answers on free plan, Slack/Sheets connections) without citing the Formkit page they come from.
Several evidence items are paraphrased, with no verbatim snippets or dates logged.
truthY: Some location and size claims (e.g., HUEMOR in Pittsburgh, Amply's 34 people) rest on single pages and may be outdated or wrong. Worth rechecking before send.
Numeric fit and timing scores (e.g., 88/100) imply precision the evidence does not support, though they are labelled as judgments.
Orbit's timing angle depends on a future application window that was not verified as open.

reasons: B delivers all 10 real, cited prospects with URLs, fit and timing scores labelled as analyst judgment, and a ready sequence with a personal first line for each. A delivers 0 sendable prospects and 4 holds against 10 requested.
B is honest about limits: it says no evidence shows any prospect is shopping, flags Orbit's applications as unverified, and avoids guessed emails.
B's pitch is consistent and tied to Formkit's confirmed features (conditional logic, drop-off reporting, custom domains).
A is very rigorous, but it is mostly process: unknown size and country, undated evidence, paraphrased snippets, and blocked sends. The owner can do almost nothing with it today.

A's sequence is decent and its first lines are specific, but only 3 of its first lines exist and none is cleared for sending. The spam-warning opener for Thirteen is a nice touch, but that prospect is blocked.

B's weaknesses: no named contacts except Bop's Jeremy Durant, mostly undated triggers, low timing scores, and agencies that may be too sophisticated or ill-fitting for Formkit. Its sequence is somewhat generic and drops the greeting and footer by design. Still far more usable than A.
truthX: Evidence observations are largely paraphrased with no verbatim snippets or dates logged, which weakens verifiability.
Claims like 'AI builds it', 'unlimited forms and responses on free' and 'Pro $6 a seat' are not cited in the output.
Offers to rebuild forms for prospects, a commitment the owner has not confirmed (the notes flag this).
truthY: Fit and timing scores are labelled as judgment but have no stated basis.
Orbit's '50+ people' and Amply's '34 people' rely on claims that are not independently verified here.
Contacts are given as roles, not people, apart from Bop's Jeremy Durant. Some role titles are guesses, though they are marked as roles.

reasons: Truth is weighted first. A ties every claim to a specific deep URL (inquiry or form pages), marks paraphrase versus verbatim, and refuses to list emails or contacts it didn't capture. It reports a 6-of-10 shortfall instead of padding the list.

B cites only homepages for very specific claims: named contacts, exact session dates, prices, '33,000 AEC customers', '200+ events'. None of it can be traced to a page. The 84/95-style fit scores show false precision.

A's ICP is sharper and fits a $6/seat form builder better. Small studios where the inquiry form is client-facing brand work suit Formkit's custom-domain, no-badge pitch. B targets large orgs (AIA NY, Main Street America, DMI) that likely run established event platforms and are unlikely to switch.
A's first lines are genuinely personal and set up the pitch. The Rocky West four-forms-to-conditional-logic line is strong. Most of B's lines just restate an event date and give no reason to care.

Against A: it delivers 0 sendable prospects and only 3 first lines. That is a real usefulness failure for a 90-day revenue goal. B is far closer to send-ready if its facts hold, so the margin is slight.
Both sequences are competent. A's has a two-variant opener, a concrete offer to rebuild their form, and good compliance notes. B's is clean, with CAN-SPAM and ICO sources, but more generic.
truthX: Product claims (AI-written replies, Claude/ChatGPT integration, partial answers on the free plan) are not linked to a Formkit source page in the deliverable.
Rocky West's Typeform link is reported as confirmed but was not opened, though A flags this itself.
truthY: Specific facts (named contacts like Sabina Khadr and Gustavo Ustariz, session dates, prices, customer and event counts) are cited only to homepages, so they cannot be verified.
Fit/timing scores like 84/95 are presented with unsupported precision, despite a caveat that they are directional.
DMI first line says the deadline is 'end of October', while the evidence column says the deadline shows Nov. 4. The line picks one side of an unresolved discrepancy.
Generic info@ addresses are listed as contacts without the specific page where each was found.

reasons: B delivers the requested 10 prospects, each with a dated trigger, a source link, a named contact where available, and a public email. A delivers 0 sendable prospects and only 4 holds.

B's first lines are specific to each prospect's observed event or form and are usable as written. A has first lines for only 3 of 4 holds, and none can be sent because size, country and email are unconfirmed.

B's sequence is concise, sells one low-risk action (a parallel test form for one event), and covers payments, logic and drop-off with product-grounded claims. A's sequence is decent, but it can't be used without prospects.
B's fit and timing scores are labelled directional estimates, and it flags the DMI date discrepancy and compliance steps honestly. A is honest about its shortfall, but the output is nearly unusable.
A's honesty and compliance rigor are admirable, but a top specialist would rather hand the owner B, which is actionable now.
truthX: Evidence 'date seen' is not logged and snippets are paraphrased, so the evidence is weak.
Item 3 of the sequence claims 'Formkit Pro can write a personal reply' and the first-line claims about the prospects' forms rest on unverified paraphrases.
truthY: Every source link is only a homepage, so the specific claims about workshop dates and prices can't be verified from the cited URLs.
Fit and timing scores such as 84/95 look falsely precise, though they are labelled estimates.
Some emails and named contacts could be unverified; the output does tell the owner to verify them.
The 'research date' of Oct 2026 and the specific workshop details are unsupported by what is cited.

climbos.topIssue: The deliverable falls far short of the job: 4 unverified holds and 0 sendable prospects against 10 requested. Size, country and contact emails are missing for every studio, so the owner cannot send a single email without redoing the research.

luna.topIssue: The personal first lines only restate a public fact without linking it to a problem Formkit solves, and the Day 0 email is a feature-and-price dump sent mostly to generic info@ inboxes, so replies and paid conversions are likely to be low. Compounding this, citations point to homepages rather than the specific event pages, and the DMI line asserts an end-of-October deadline the research itself flagged as unverified.

sol.topIssue: The list pitches sophisticated web agencies on replacing their own low-volume contact forms, a weak paid use case with mostly self-admitted low timing scores, while ignoring the stronger angle of agencies deploying Formkit across client sites. It pairs this with a bland, feature-led sequence that has weak or missing CTAs and only one named contact.
